deleterious

del-ih-TEER-ee-us -- from Greek dēlētērios ('noxious'), rooted in deleisthai ('to hurt, injure'). · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Deleterious is causing harm or damage, especially in a gradual or not-immediately-obvious way.

The nutritionist explained that a diet heavy in processed sugar could have a deleterious effect on a growing child's energy levels.

Example

Years of construction dust turned out to have a deleterious effect on the workers' lung health, even though none of them felt sick at first.

The harm builds up slowly and isn't obvious right away -- exactly the kind of gradual, damaging effect deleterious describes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

unhealthy: Unhealthy means bad for the body -- an unhealthy diet, unhealthy air, an unhealthy habit. It is an everyday word tied to health. Deleterious is its formal, scientific cousin and ranges wider: a chemical, a policy, or a rumor can be deleterious to an ecosystem, an economy, or a reputation.

counterproductive: Counterproductive describes an action that defeats its own purpose -- cramming all night is counterproductive because it lowers the very test score it was meant to raise. Deleterious is about the damage itself, usually to health, an environment, or a system, whether or not anyone had a goal at all.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

beneficial: producing good or helpful results

salutary: having a good or wholesome effect

Where it sits · how serious the damage is

harmful → deleterious → detrimental

harmful vs. deleterious: Harmful is milder than deleterious: late-night screen time is mildly harmful to sleep, but a deleterious habit does deeper damage that creeps up before anyone notices it.

detrimental vs. deleterious: Detrimental is graver than deleterious: a deleterious effect is real but often so gradual that only careful study reveals it, while damage called detrimental is serious enough that no one disputes the harm.

Build the Word

The pieces

Put it together: Deleterious traces back to Greek deleisthai, 'to hurt or injure' -- a deleter was a destroyer. Unlike many Greek roots, this one never went on to build other common English words.

Use the root in a new word: deleterious effect: Deleterious almost always appears paired with the word effect or effects in formal writing -- 'a deleterious effect on the ecosystem' is far more common than deleterious used alone.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Deleterious is a formal, often scientific word -- it's most at home describing measurable harm to health, the environment, or a system, rather than everyday unpleasantness.
